title: A worked example's numbers never replace the creator's numbers
text: Worked cases carry numbers that fitted another brief: a 150 s limit, a 5 x 5 m floor, 5 checkpoints. When the creator has given a number for the same thing (minutes per play, players at once, floor size, time of day), the creator's number is the answer and the example only shows the shape of a good design. In a blind review a 3-minute brief became a 150 s game because a case card said so.
use_when: A retrieved case or default states a number that the brief also states.
do: Copy the brief's number into the plan first, then read the cards
Use a case for its structure and its lesson, not its figures
avoid: Taking a time limit, player count or light preset from a case when the brief gives one
source: Land Builder design sessions: blind review of 20 design conversations by two AI models, 19 Nov 2026 (Songkran brief)

title: A turn is play time plus handover: keep them as two numbers
text: At an event one turn has two parts: the play itself and the handover (wipe the headset, fit it, explain the rule). When the creator says how long one play lasts, that is the game's time limit. Handover is planned on top of it, usually 30 to 60 s, and belongs in the staff plan and the queue estimate, not in the game timer. Shortening the game to make room for handover changes what the creator asked for.
use_when: Setting timeLimit for a booth, a class or any place where players take turns.
do: timeLimit = the creator's minutes per play, in seconds
Add handover time to the throughput estimate (players per hour)
avoid: Cutting the timer below the creator's play length to fit a turn
source: Land Builder design sessions: blind review of 20 design conversations by two AI models, 19 Nov 2026 (Songkran brief)

title: A space or night theme in a daylit room: carry it with models and colour, not with darkness
text: A solar system, a deep sea or a night market asks for darkness, but the room is a gym in the morning with windows. In passthrough the real light stays, so a night preset only makes the virtual floor and models look dim against a bright room. Keep a bright preset (morning, studio, default) and carry the theme with the models, a dark floor texture, strong colour contrast and labels. Use night, spooky or neon only when the real room is dark or the creator asks for it.
use_when: The theme suggests darkness but the brief says daytime, windows or outdoors.
do: Match the preset to the real light
Let planets, lanterns or glowing props be bright objects on a dark floor
avoid: A night preset because the theme is space
Glow effects as the main read in daylight
source: Land Builder design sessions: blind review of 20 design conversations by two AI models, 19 Nov 2026 (school gym brief)

title: Several racers on one real floor: one measured cell per player
text: In a race every player walks their own copy of the Land, but they all stand on the same real floor. If each copy covers the whole floor the players cross each other blind. Split the floor into one cell per player: keep 0.6 m clear at the edge and 1 m between cells, and make every cell at least 2 x 2 m. A 10 x 10 m courtyard gives four cells of 3.9 x 3.9 m. Design the route for one cell and repeat it. If the cells come out under 2 m, fewer players walk at once and the rest wait their turn.
use_when: play_mode is race and more than one player walks at the same time in one real space.
do: Work out the cells from the floor size before choosing the route
Write the cell size in the layout brief
Mark cell borders on the real floor with tape or cones
avoid: One route across the whole floor for every racer
Assuming a floor is big enough without measuring
source: Land Builder design sessions: blind review of 20 design conversations by two AI models, 19 Nov 2026 (multiplayer layouts were unproven in both conditions)

title: A shared route: start players apart and keep 2 m between them
text: When several players walk one shared route they bunch up at checkpoints and hazards. Plan about 6 square metres of usable floor per player, start them 2 m apart or a few seconds after each other, and say in the rules that everyone keeps two steps behind the player in front. Make checkpoints wide enough for the group to gather beside the route, not on it.
use_when: play_mode is together with 2 or more players on one floor.
do: Staggered start
A rule about distance, in plain words
Gathering spots beside the route
avoid: Four players released at once into a 1.2 m corridor
source: Land Builder design sessions: blind review of 20 design conversations by two AI models, 19 Nov 2026 (school gym brief)

title: Older players: build rest into the route as a story stop
text: A calm walk for older adults still tires them: the headset is heavy and standing still is harder than walking. Make one or two checkpoints rest stops with a story reason (a tea stall, a bench by the market) where the label invites a pause, place a real chair just outside the area at that point, and let the helper offer a rest there. With no time limit a rest costs nothing. Plans in the review had wide spacing and a seated alternative but no moment that invited a rest.
use_when: Players are older adults, or anyone who may need to pause during a walking game.
do: Name a rest stop in the checkpoint labels
A real chair beside that stop, outside the play area
timeLimit null
avoid: A timer or time bonus that punishes resting
Rest only before or after the play
source: Land Builder design sessions: blind review of 20 design conversations by two AI models, 19 Nov 2026 (seniors centre brief, gap named by both reviewers)

title: A timed race needs an ending for players who do not finish
text: With a time limit some players, often first-timers and children, are still on the route when time runs out. Plan that ending: the score they reached counts and shows on the leaderboard, the last screen says how far they got in kind words, and the helper knows to walk them out. Put the best moment of the game before the last third of the route so slow players still meet it.
use_when: A runner with timeLimit set and mixed or first-time players.
do: Say in the rules that the score at time-out counts
Place the key moment by two thirds of the route
A kind time-out line on the last card
avoid: The climax at the portal only
source: Land Builder design sessions: blind review of 20 design conversations by two AI models, 19 Nov 2026 (gap named by both reviewers)

title: In a planning puzzle, a faster beat adds reflex, not depth
text: The beat is the time between guard moves. Making the last board hard by cutting the beat to 1.5 s turns a planning game into a reaction game, and players who came to think lose to the clock. When the creator asks for a hard puzzle, raise difficulty with more guards, longer capture orders, cracked squares and a harder piece, and keep the beat at 3 s or more. Use a short beat only when the creator asks for speed.
use_when: Tuning the difficulty of tactics boards for players who want challenge through planning.
do: Harder boards through layout: guards, order, cracks, piece
Beat 3 s or more for planning games
avoid: A 1.5 to 2 s beat as the main difficulty step
source: Land Builder design sessions: blind review of 20 design conversations by two AI models, 19 Nov 2026 (PC chess brief, where the design without cards was preferred)

title: State the game's numbers once, then repeat them unchanged
text: Designs drift between steps: the option says six stops, the sketch draws two hazards, the plan asks for four. Each drift is small and each one costs trust when the creator notices. Write the numbers of the game once in the prototype (stops, hazards, time limit, players at once, light) and repeat exactly those in the storyboard, the sketch, the rules and the layout brief. If a number must change, change it in one place and say so.
use_when: Writing a prototype and the build plan that follows it.
do: One list of numbers in the prototype
Draw every hazard in the sketch
Same seconds in the rules as in the timer
avoid: A new count in a later step without telling the creator
source: Land Builder design sessions: blind review of 20 design conversations by two AI models, 19 Nov 2026 (mall booth brief)

title: Give each requested feeling a moment, and the main one the climax
text: A design can be safe and specific and still miss the feeling the creator asked for: a discovery game whose climax is a dodge, a together game where nobody needs anybody. For every feeling in the brief name the moment that delivers it and what the player does there. The climax delivers the first feeling on the list. A feeling without a moment is a reason to change the storyboard, not to drop the feeling.
use_when: Writing the storyboard and choosing the climax.
do: One named beat per requested feeling
Climax serves the first feeling
Say what the player does in that beat
avoid: A generic exciting climax that fits no requested feeling
source: Land Builder design sessions: blind review of 20 design conversations by two AI models, 19 Nov 2026 (birthday and school briefs)
